Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 64, verse 7–18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve claim﴾. Ibn 'Umar used to say: "Za'amu" (they claimed) is an expression of falsehood. And Mujahid disliked that a man say: "Za'ama fulan" (so-and-so claimed).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that is easy for Allah﴾. It means the Resurrection (al-ba'th). "The light" is the Qur'an, and in it is the clarification of the matter of the Resurrection, the Reckoning and the Recompense.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Day He gathers you﴾ is in the accusative governed by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will surely be resurrected, then you will surely be informed of what you did﴾, and ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection. It was so named because Allah, may He be exalted, gathers in it the jinn and mankind, the inhabitants of the heavens and the inhabitants of the earth. ﴿That is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain﴾. "Taghabun" is a reciprocal form from "ghabn" (loss in a transaction), which is the missing of a share. Regarding its being named the Day of Resurrection the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain, there are four views.

The first: there is no disbeliever except that he has a dwelling and a family in Paradise, and that believer inherits it, so the disbeliever is then defrauded. Abu Salih reported this meaning from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the defrauding of the people of Paradise of the people of the Fire; this was said by Mujahid and al-Qurazi. The third: that it is the day of the wronged person defrauding the wrongdoer, because the wronged person was defrauded in the world, so in the Hereafter he becomes the one who defrauds; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The fourth: that it is a day in which the disbeliever's loss becomes manifest through his abandoning faith, and the believer's loss through his shortcoming in good deeds; this was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Al-Zajjaj said: "This was mentioned as an example of buying and selling, like His saying: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16], and His saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce?﴾ [al-Saff: 10]." What follows this is clear, up to His saying: ﴿He will remove from him his misdeeds﴾. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "nukaffir" and "wa-nudkhiluhu" with the letter nun in both. The rest read them with the letter ya'. ﴿No calamity strikes except by the permission of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "By His knowledge and decree." ﴿And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart﴾. Regarding this there are six views.

The first: He guides his heart to certainty, so he knows that what befell him would not have missed him, and what missed him would not have befallen him; this was narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Alqamah said: it is the man who is struck by a calamity and knows that it is from Allah, may He be exalted, so he submits and is content.

The second: He guides his heart to "istirja'" (saying: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return"); this was said by Muqatil.

The third: that when he is tested he is patient, when he is blessed he is thankful, and when he is wronged he forgives; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Ibn Qutaybah.

The fourth: He guides his heart, that is, makes it guided; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The fifth: [He guides his protector (waliyy) with patience and contentment; this was said by Abu Bakr al-Warraq. The sixth: ] He guides his heart to follow the Sunnah when his faith is sound; this was said by Abu 'Uthman al-Hiyari. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Abu Nuhayk read "yahda" with an open ya' and a fatha on the dal, with "qalbuhu" in the nominative. Al-Zajjaj said: this is from hada'a, yahda'u, meaning "to become calm." So the meaning is: when he submits to the command of Allah, his heart is calm. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, al-Dahhak, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and al-Azraq from Hamzah read "nahdi" with a nun. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "yuhda" with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the dal, with "qalbuhu" in the nominative.

What follows this is clear, up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you﴾. The occasion of its revelation: a man would embrace Islam, and when he intended to emigrate, his family and children would prevent him, saying: "We implore you by Allah not to go and leave your family and your tribe and go to Medina without family or wealth." Among them were some who were moved by pity for them and remained without emigrating, so this verse was revealed. When those (who had been prevented) emigrated, and saw that the people had gained understanding in the religion, they resolved to punish their families who had prevented them, so Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿And if you pardon and overlook﴾ to the end of the verse. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: when they intended to emigrate, their wives and children said to them: "We have endured for your sake the separation from the religion, but we cannot endure your separation from us, and the separation from wealth and dwellings." So Allah, mighty and majestic, informed that whoever is in this condition is an enemy, even if he is a child or a wife. Regarding this spending there are three views.

The first: charity; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: a believer's spending on himself; this was said by al-Hasan. The third: spending in jihad; this was said by al-Dahhak. ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul﴾ until he gives the right of Allah from his wealth. The explanation of this has already preceded in [al-Hashr: 9], and what follows it has already been explained up to the end of the surah [al-Baqarah: 254; al-Hadid: 18, 11; al-Hashr: 24, 23].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 64, verse 7–18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve claim﴾. Ibn 'Umar used to say: "Za'amu" (they claimed) is an expression of falsehood. And Mujahid disliked that a man say: "Za'ama fulan" (so-and-so claimed).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that is easy for Allah﴾. It means the Resurrection (al-ba'th). "The light" is the Qur'an, and in it is the clarification of the matter of the Resurrection, the Reckoning and the Recompense.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Day He gathers you﴾ is in the accusative governed by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will surely be resurrected, then you will surely be informed of what you did﴾, and ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection. It was so named because Allah, may He be exalted, gathers in it the jinn and mankind, the inhabitants of the heavens and the inhabitants of the earth. ﴿That is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain﴾. "Taghabun" is a reciprocal form from "ghabn" (loss in a transaction), which is the missing of a share. Regarding its being named the Day of Resurrection the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain, there are four views.

The first: there is no disbeliever except that he has a dwelling and a family in Paradise, and that believer inherits it, so the disbeliever is then defrauded. Abu Salih reported this meaning from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the defrauding of the people of Paradise of the people of the Fire; this was said by Mujahid and al-Qurazi. The third: that it is the day of the wronged person defrauding the wrongdoer, because the wronged person was defrauded in the world, so in the Hereafter he becomes the one who defrauds; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The fourth: that it is a day in which the disbeliever's loss becomes manifest through his abandoning faith, and the believer's loss through his shortcoming in good deeds; this was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Al-Zajjaj said: "This was mentioned as an example of buying and selling, like His saying: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16], and His saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce?﴾ [al-Saff: 10]." What follows this is clear, up to His saying: ﴿He will remove from him his misdeeds﴾. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "nukaffir" and "wa-nudkhiluhu" with the letter nun in both. The rest read them with the letter ya'. ﴿No calamity strikes except by the permission of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "By His knowledge and decree." ﴿And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart﴾. Regarding this there are six views.

The first: He guides his heart to certainty, so he knows that what befell him would not have missed him, and what missed him would not have befallen him; this was narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Alqamah said: it is the man who is struck by a calamity and knows that it is from Allah, may He be exalted, so he submits and is content.

The second: He guides his heart to "istirja'" (saying: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return"); this was said by Muqatil.

The third: that when he is tested he is patient, when he is blessed he is thankful, and when he is wronged he forgives; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Ibn Qutaybah.

The fourth: He guides his heart, that is, makes it guided; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The fifth: [He guides his protector (waliyy) with patience and contentment; this was said by Abu Bakr al-Warraq. The sixth: ] He guides his heart to follow the Sunnah when his faith is sound; this was said by Abu 'Uthman al-Hiyari. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Abu Nuhayk read "yahda" with an open ya' and a fatha on the dal, with "qalbuhu" in the nominative. Al-Zajjaj said: this is from hada'a, yahda'u, meaning "to become calm." So the meaning is: when he submits to the command of Allah, his heart is calm. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, al-Dahhak, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and al-Azraq from Hamzah read "nahdi" with a nun. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "yuhda" with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the dal, with "qalbuhu" in the nominative.

What follows this is clear, up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you﴾. The occasion of its revelation: a man would embrace Islam, and when he intended to emigrate, his family and children would prevent him, saying: "We implore you by Allah not to go and leave your family and your tribe and go to Medina without family or wealth." Among them were some who were moved by pity for them and remained without emigrating, so this verse was revealed. When those (who had been prevented) emigrated, and saw that the people had gained understanding in the religion, they resolved to punish their families who had prevented them, so Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿And if you pardon and overlook﴾ to the end of the verse. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: when they intended to emigrate, their wives and children said to them: "We have endured for your sake the separation from the religion, but we cannot endure your separation from us, and the separation from wealth and dwellings." So Allah, mighty and majestic, informed that whoever is in this condition is an enemy, even if he is a child or a wife. Mujahid said: the man's love for his child and wife would lead him to sever his kinship ties and disobey his Lord. Qatadah said: among their spouses and children were those who forbade them from Islam and discouraged them from it. Regarding His saying: ﴿an enemy to you﴾ there are three views.

The first: by preventing him from emigrating; this is according to the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: by their being a cause of sins; according to this is the saying of Mujahid. The third: by their forbidding him from Islam; this is according to the saying of Qatadah.

His saying: ﴿So beware of them﴾. Al-Farra' said: do not obey them in staying behind.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾, that is, a test and a preoccupation from the Hereafter. Wealth and children lead one into grave matters, except for whom Allah protects. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, a burden (ighram). It is said: "Fulan was tried (futina) with the woman," and "shughifa biha," meaning he was infatuated with her. Al-Farra' said: the people of meanings said: "min" entered in His saying: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses﴾ because not all spouses and children are enemies. "Min" was not mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ because they are never free of trial and the heart's preoccupation with them. Buraydah narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was delivering a sermon when al-Hasan and al-Husayn came, wearing two red shirts, walking and stumbling. He descended from the minbar, carried them, placed them before him, and then said: "Allah, mighty and majestic, has spoken the truth: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾. I looked at these two boys walking and stumbling, and I could not be patient until I interrupted my speech and lifted them."
